```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Two decisions shape a semantic topic model before any topic is read: how
many topics the texts are divided into, and what unit of text is
divided. Neither has a correct value that can be estimated from the data.
k-means (Lloyd, 1982) partitions the embeddings into as many groups as it
is asked for, and every additional group captures more of their
variation, so a fit criterion alone always prefers more topics. The unit matters as much: a
document that does several things at once can belong to only one topic,
while its sentences can belong to different ones.

This guide treats both decisions as comparisons. Candidate models are
fitted on the same embeddings and compared on measures of their quality,
and the candidates the measures favor are then examined for topics that
duplicate one another. The measures inform the choice; the representative
texts of the candidates decide it.

```{r setup}
library(sbert)
```

## Data

The analysis uses the first 600 distinct feedback messages of
`feedback_translations`, whose sentence embeddings ship with the package
as `feedback_embeddings` (row *i* of the matrix embeds row *i* of
`corpus`), so every model below is fitted without downloading a model.

- **`translation`:** the English text of each message; the modeled text.
- **`n`:** the number of times the message occurs in the full corpus,
  added by `dedupe()`.
- **`feedback_embeddings`:** a 600 by 384 matrix of `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`
  embeddings, one row per message.

```{r data}
corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"), 600)
dim(feedback_embeddings)
```

## How do the candidate counts compare?

`compare_topics()` fits one model for every candidate number of topics on
one shared set of embeddings, and keeps the fitted models. The candidates
here run from 3 to 20 topics:

```{r sweep}
sweep <- compare_topics(corpus, column = "translation",
                        n_topics = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20),
                        embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
sweep
```

Each row reports three measures and a convergence flag.

- `explained` is the share of the variation in the embeddings that lies
  between topics, the between-topic sum of squares over the total. It is
  the only measure computed from the embeddings. It rises from 0.111 with
  three topics to 0.351 with twenty, and it can only rise: a partition into
  more groups can always reproduce a coarser one and then split a group
  further, which lowers the within-topic variation. It describes how much
  structure each count captures, never which count to use.
- `coherence` is the mean normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI;
  Bouma, 2009) of each topic's top ten terms: whether the words that
  describe a topic occur together in the same messages. It lies between
  -1 and 1, and higher is better.
- `topic_diversity` is the share of distinct words among the pooled top-ten
  lists of all topics (Dieng et al., 2020). It is 1 when no two topics
  share a top word, and it falls as topics begin to repeat each other's
  vocabulary.
- `converged` records whether k-means reached a stable partition within
  `iter_max` iterations (default 100). A candidate that did not converge
  also raises a warning of class `sbert_no_converge`, and its measures
  describe an unfinished partition. Every candidate here converged.

Coherence is negative at every count, because the messages are short and
two content words rarely occur in the same message. It does not fall
steadily as topics are added: it has a local peak at six topics (-0.104),
a second at eight (-0.118), and reaches its highest values at fifteen
(-0.0979) and twenty (-0.0994). Topic diversity falls from 0.940 at five
topics to 0.733 at twenty, a first sign that the larger models describe
several topics with the same words.

`summary()` states the most coherent candidate in one row, together with
whether every candidate converged:

```{r sweep-summary}
summary(sweep)
```

`plot()` draws the three measures against the number of topics, with a
dotted line at the most coherent candidate:

```{r sweep-plot}
plot(sweep)
```

The plot shows the pattern that makes the highest coherence a poor rule.
Between three and twelve topics the curve has a clear maximum at six;
beyond twelve, coherence climbs again while diversity drops. The next two
sections ask why.

## Why do small topics flatter the mean coherence?

The coherence of a candidate is the plain mean over its topics, so a topic
of three messages counts as much as a topic of a hundred and sixty.
`fitted()` takes the fifteen-topic model out of the comparison without
refitting it, and `summary()` lists the size and coherence of every topic:

```{r summary-15}
model_15 <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 15)
summary(model_15)
```

The fifteen topics range from 162 messages to 2. The three smallest hold 8,
3 and 2 messages, and the most coherent topic of the model (0.421) is the
one with 8 messages, all built around one instruction (*Find the train
that makes the sound with the number...*). Three of the four largest
topics, which hold most of the messages, have negative coherence (-0.150
to -0.392). The plain mean therefore describes the small topics
more than the corpus.

`coherence_weight = "size"` weights each topic's coherence by its number
of messages, so that a tiny topic of near-identical texts cannot decide
the comparison:

```{r sweep-weighted}
sweep_weighted <- compare_topics(corpus, column = "translation",
                                 n_topics = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20),
                                 embeddings = feedback_embeddings,
                                 coherence_weight = "size")
sweep_weighted
```

Weighting lowers the coherence of every candidate, because in every model
the coherent topics are the small ones: for fifteen topics it moves from
-0.0979 to -0.180, for six from -0.104 to -0.216. Up to twelve topics the
weighted measure still peaks at six. Above twelve it still rises, to -0.180
at fifteen and -0.166 at twenty. Weighting removes the influence of the
tiny topics, and on this corpus that is not what drives coherence up at
high counts; the next section shows what does. The same weighting is
available for a single model as `coherence(model, weight = "size")`.

## Is a count too fine?

A count is too fine when it splits one kind of text into topics that
differ only in wording. `topic_hierarchy()` measures the cosine distance
between the topic centers and merges the closest topics step by step;
`summary()` gives each topic its nearest neighbor:

```{r hierarchy-15}
tree_15 <- topic_hierarchy(model_15)
summary(tree_15)
```

Several pairs lie much closer to each other than to anything else.
Topics 3 and 8 (0.170 apart) are both questions of the form *What does
"all the ones between X and Y" mean?*, differing in whether the message
says "all the ones between" or "all between". Topics 2 and 6 (0.183) are
the same short hint with the same two phrasings. Topics 1 and 9 (0.220)
share the phrase "all the pictures between", once in an instruction and
once inside a question about its meaning. The first two splits follow
wording, not what the message does for the learner, and splits of this
kind explain the rise of coherence at high counts: a topic restricted
to one phrasing has top words that always occur together. The fifteen-topic
model is too fine for a question about kinds of feedback.

The same diagnosis applied to the six-topic model:

```{r hierarchy-6}
model_6 <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 6)
tree_6 <- topic_hierarchy(model_6)
summary(tree_6)
plot(tree_6)
```

The closest pair in the six-topic model is 0.297 apart: questions about
the meaning of a phrase (topic 3) and definitions of a phrase (topic 5).
They concern meaning, but one asks the learner and the other tells them,
which is a distinction of function rather than of wording. The six topics
are not near-duplicates of one another.

## Can merging recover a coarser model?

`reduce_topics()` merges the topics of a fitted model along the hierarchy,
without refitting k-means. Merging the fifteen topics into twelve folds
exactly the three near-duplicate pairs found above:

```{r reduce-12}
topic_sizes(reduce_topics(model_15, n_topics = 12))
```

Merging is suited to removing such duplicates. It is not a substitute for
fitting a smaller count directly. Merged down to six topics, the fifteen
topics become one topic of 457 messages, two of 88 and 42, and three of
8, 3 and 2:

```{r reduce-6}
merged_6 <- reduce_topics(model_15, n_topics = 6)
topic_sizes(merged_6)
```

The hierarchy merges the closest centers first, so the main kinds of
feedback, which lie close together, are merged with each other, while the
small topics far from everything else survive to the end. The
cross-tabulation of the merged model against the six-topic k-means fit
shows how differently the two divide the same messages:

```{r reduce-compare}
assignments <- merge(as.data.frame(model_6), as.data.frame(merged_6),
                     by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_kmeans", "_merged"))
with(assignments, table(topic_kmeans, topic_merged))
```

The first merged topic absorbs most of k-means topics 1, 2 and 3. To move
to a much smaller count, fit it with `compare_topics()` or `topics()`;
use `reduce_topics()` for the last few merges of near-duplicate topics.

## Should the unit be the document or the sentence?

The second decision is the unit that is embedded and clustered. A model at
the document level gives each document one topic. A model at the sentence
level embeds every sentence, so a document that hints and then corrects
contributes one sentence to each topic, and `topic_gamma()` reports the
share of each topic in each document (see
[Assigning new documents and topic mixtures](assigning-topics.html)).
Sentences are also short enough to be read in full by the encoder, which
reads at most 256 tokens of a text with the default model; long documents
are truncated.

`segment()` splits text into sentences without a model, which shows how
much the unit would change for these messages:

```{r sentences}
sentences <- with(corpus, segment(translation, level = "sentence"))
nrow(sentences)
with(sentences, table(segment))
```

The 600 messages hold 781 sentences: 177 messages have a second sentence
and 4 a third. Most messages are single sentences, so for this corpus the
document is a natural unit. For long texts, such as research abstracts,
the choice changes what a topic is.

`compare_topics()` compares both units in one call when `segment` names
both levels. Every candidate count is fitted at every level, and
`fitted()` takes `segment =` to pick one. The sentence embeddings are not
bundled with the package, so the chunk below needs a downloaded model and
is not run here:

```{r levels, eval = FALSE}
model_download()
levels <- compare_topics(corpus, column = "translation",
                         n_topics = c(4, 6, 8, 10),
                         segment = c("document", "sentence"))
summary(levels)
plot(levels)
sentence_model <- fitted(levels, n_topics = 6, segment = "sentence")
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
```

`summary(levels)` gives the most coherent count per level, and
`plot(levels)` draws one line per level, told apart by color, point shape
and line type. With precomputed embeddings, `embeddings` takes a list of
matrices named by level, such as
`list(document = feedback_embeddings, sentence = sentence_embeddings)`,
whose sentence matrix has one row per row of `segment(..., level =
"sentence")`. The coherence of the two levels is computed on different
units, so a comparison between levels rests on reading their topics more
than on their numbers. Splitting long documents, merging short fragments
and capping segment length are covered in
[Segmenting long documents](segmenting.html).

## When to use which

| Question | Verb |
|----------|------|
| How do candidate counts compare? | `compare_topics()`, `plot(sweep)` |
| Which candidate is most coherent? | `summary(sweep)` |
| Do small topics drive the comparison? | `compare_topics(coherence_weight = "size")`, `summary(model)` |
| Did every candidate converge? | the `converged` column |
| Are some topics near-duplicates? | `topic_hierarchy()`, `summary(tree)`, `plot(tree)` |
| Merge near-duplicates without refitting | `reduce_topics()` |
| Use one candidate | `fitted(sweep, n_topics = )` |
| Documents or sentences? | `compare_topics(segment = c("document", "sentence"))` |

The six-topic model chosen here is read and named in
[Describing and naming topics](describing-topics.html), and the full
analysis is in [Semantic topic modeling with Sentence-BERT](sbert.html).
